Specular reflection¶

Summary¶

Reflection finds the specular reflection point of the GNSS signal on the Earth’s surface for one transmitting GNSS satellite and one receiving LEO satellite, at every time sample in the propagated window. It is the geometry engine of the forward-scatter path: for each sample it solves where the bounce lands, the incidence angle there, and – with a link-budget configuration – the received power. Coverage builds one Reflection per (LEO, GNSS) pair to accumulate revisit counts; the moving-target detector uses the same geometry per Tx/Rx pair.

The specular point is the surface point \(S\) for which the incoming ray \(T\!\to\!S\) and the outgoing ray \(S\!\to\!R\) make equal angles with the local surface normal (the law of reflection). Two solvers implement this:

  • spherical – a closed-form solution: rotate into the Tx-Rx orbital plane and solve a quartic on the circle;

  • elliptical – solve the two tangent components of Fermat’s stationary-path condition on a two-angle WGS-84 surface parameterisation, then verify the specular condition.

Detailed Module Description¶

Central-angle gate and line of sight¶

Before any solve, two cheap filters reject samples that cannot produce a reflection. The Tx-Rx geocentric central angle

(45)¶\[\theta_c = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{r}_{tx}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{rx}} {\lVert\mathbf{r}_{tx}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{r}_{rx}\rVert}\right)\]

must be below max_central_angle_deg. Line of sight is tested analytically on the finite chord between the two satellites,

(46)¶\[\mathbf{P}(t) = \mathbf{r}_1 + t\,(\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1), \quad t\in[0,1],\]

by projecting the origin onto the chord, clamping the parameter to \([0,1]\), and requiring that closest point to clear the Earth. For WGS-84, each coordinate is first scaled by \((a,a,b)\), mapping the ellipsoid to a unit sphere. This catches grazing intersections without sampling error and avoids the overly conservative equatorial-sphere approximation near the poles.

Law of reflection¶

With the incoming and outgoing unit propagation directions and the outward surface normal at \(S\),

(47)¶\[\hat{v}_{in} = \frac{S - T}{\lVert S - T\rVert}, \qquad \hat{v}_{out} = \frac{R - S}{\lVert R - S\rVert}, \qquad \hat{n} = \hat{n}(S),\]

the specular condition is that the specularly reflected incoming ray equals the outgoing ray:

(48)¶\[\hat{v}_{refl} = \hat{v}_{in} - 2\,(\hat{v}_{in}\cdot\hat{n})\,\hat{n}, \qquad \mathbf{e}(S) = \hat{v}_{refl} - \hat{v}_{out} = \mathbf{0}.\]

Equivalently the incidence and reflected angles measured from the normal are equal,

(49)¶\[\cos\left(\theta_{in}\right) = -\,\hat{v}_{in}\cdot\hat{n}, \qquad \cos\left(\theta_{out}\right) = \hat{v}_{out}\cdot\hat{n}, \qquad \theta_{in} = \theta_{out}.\]

The stored incidence angle refl_ang_vec is the mean of \(\theta_{in}\) and \(\theta_{out}\) (equal at a converged solution).

Spherical solver (FreeFlyer method)¶

For a sphere the problem is planar. The geometry is rotated so the Tx-Rx plane becomes \(z = 0\) (object_definitions.Reflection_def.Reflection.get_rotation_3D_to_plane_coords()), reducing it to two dimensions. Writing the reflection point as a combination of the normalised satellite and GNSS vectors \(A = \mathbf{r}_{rx}/R_\oplus\), \(B = \mathbf{r}_{tx}/R_\oplus\) and \(N = x\,A + y\,B\), the law of reflection collapses to a quartic in \(x\),

(50)¶\[r_4 x^4 + r_3 x^3 + r_2 x^2 + r_1 x + r_0 = 0,\]

with coefficients in \(u = A\cdot A\), \(v = A\cdot B\), \(w = B\cdot B\),

(51)¶\[\begin{split}\begin{aligned} r_0 &= w - 1, & r_1 &= 2(w - v), & r_2 &= u + 2v + w - 4uw,\\ r_3 &= 4(v^2 - uw), & r_4 &= 4u(uw - v^2). & \end{aligned}\end{split}\]

The physical root is the real, positive \(x\) whose partner

(52)¶\[y = \frac{1 + x - 2u x^2}{1 + 2v x}\]

is also positive; the point is then scaled back to the sphere and rotated into 3-D. This is exact and fast.

Elliptical solver (stationary path on a parameterised surface)¶

On the WGS-84 ellipsoid there is no such closed form, so the specular point is found by Fermat’s principle – the reflected ray has stationary optical length. The surface is parameterised by two angles,

(53)¶\[S(\varphi,\lambda) = \left(a\cos\varphi\cos\lambda,\ a\cos\varphi\sin\lambda,\ b\sin\varphi\right),\]

with semi-axes \(a = R_{eq}\) and \(b = a(1-f)\). Consequently every solver iterate lies on the ellipsoid. For

(54)¶\[L(S) = \lVert S-T\rVert + \lVert R-S\rVert,\]

the solver sets the two tangent components of the path gradient to zero,

(55)¶\[\nabla_S L\cdot\widehat{S_\varphi}=0,\qquad \nabla_S L\cdot\widehat{S_\lambda}=0.\]

The outward ellipsoid normal at the solution is

(56)¶\[\hat{n}(S) = \frac{(S_x/a^2,\; S_y/a^2,\; S_z/b^2)}{\lVert(S_x/a^2,\; S_y/a^2,\; S_z/b^2)\rVert}.\]

scipy.optimize.least_squares solves these two dimensionless residuals. The candidate is accepted only if it faces both satellites (\(\cos\theta_{in}>0\) and \(\cos\theta_{out}>0\)) and the independent vector reflection residual (48) satisfies \(\lVert\mathbf{e}(S)\rVert \le 5\times10^{-2}\) (a coarse acceptance gate; well-posed geometries converge far tighter, as the tests show). The spherical solution seeds the solve.

Module Assumptions and Limitations¶

  • Specular geometry only. This module locates the specular reflection point and incidence angle; the scattered power (coherent specular plus incoherent glistening zone) is the OceanTarget model, invoked through the link budget. Diffuse multipath and the finite glistening zone are not represented here.

  • Ideal reference surface. Visibility and reflection use either the configured sphere or smooth WGS-84 ellipsoid. Terrain, geoid undulation, ice and atmospheric refraction are absent.

  • Coarse central-angle pre-filter. max_central_angle_deg only removes far geometries cheaply; it is not the physical horizon limit.

  • One Tx-Rx pair per object. A constellation sweep builds many Reflection objects.

  • Array layout. Reflection points are stored (n, 3) / (n, 2) while satellite states are (3, n) (a transpose clean-up is noted in the source TODOs).

Validation and Tests¶

Test group

What it pins

test_reflection.py :: TestReflectionConstruction

Default earth_model is spherical; explicit models accepted; invalid model, missing satellite IDs and missing max_central_angle_deg all raise.

test_reflection_geometry.py :: TestCheckLosSatellites

Same-side geometry has line of sight; antipodal / far-side and grazing-intersection geometries are blocked analytically; the scaled-coordinate ellipsoid test distinguishes a valid polar grazing chord from the larger equatorial sphere.

... :: TestGetRotation3DToPlaneCoords

The plane rotation is orthogonal with determinant 1 and flattens the orbital plane onto \(z = 0\).

... :: TestGetReflectionPoint2D / TestGetReflectionPointFf

The reflection lands on the sphere and in the orbital plane; returns NaN with no line of sight; the law of reflection holds (\(\theta_{in} = \theta_{out}\)); symmetric and exactly collinear same-side geometries are finite and reflect on the symmetry axis.

... :: TestFindSpecularPointEllipseEcef

The point satisfies the ellipsoid constraint to floating-point precision and the incidence/reflection angle mismatch is below 1e-7 deg for tested geometries.

... :: TestSphericalVsEllipticalAgreement

The two solvers agree within a few km (< 20 km) and both keep an equatorial reflection in \(z = 0\).

User Guide¶

Reflection is built internally by the analysis drivers, one per (GNSS, LEO) pair; the relevant INI knobs live in [REFLECTION].

Table 13: [REFLECTION] keys¶

Key

Meaning

reflection_type

"specular" selects this specular-reflection path (vs "backscatter", the BRP path).

max_central_angle_deg

The constructor’s max_central_angle_deg geometric gate.

 
import numpy as np
from object_definitions.Reflection_def import Reflection

refl = Reflection(
    tx_satID="GPS-07",
    rx_satID="LEO-1",
    earth_model="elliptical",
    max_central_angle_deg=45.0,
)

# GNSS_state / Sat_state are propagated Satellite objects sharing the time vector `times`.
refl.compute_reflection_coordinates(
    GNSS_state=gnss_sat,
    Sat_state=leo_sat,
    times=times,
    tx_eirp_dbw=27.0,           # from Constants.GNSS_EIRP_DBW
    frequency_hz=1.57542e9,     # GPS L1
    link_budget_settings=settings,
)
reflections_eci = refl.refl_ECI_vec   # (n, 3), NaN where no reflection
incidence_deg = refl.refl_ang_vec     # (n,)

Public interface¶

class object_definitions.Reflection_def.Reflection(tx_satID=None, rx_satID=None, earth_model=None, *, max_central_angle_deg, gnss_const=None)[source]¶

Specular reflections for one (Tx GNSS, Rx LEO) satellite pair over a time window.

One Reflection holds every specular reflection produced by a single transmitting GNSS satellite and a single receiving LEO satellite across the propagated time vector. The specular point is solved per earth_model – a closed-form spherical solver or a two-angle ellipsoid stationarity solve – and, when a link-budget configuration is supplied, the received power is evaluated at each reflection.

Parameters:

  • tx_satID (Any) – Transmitting (GNSS) satellite identifier.

  • rx_satID (Any) – Receiving (LEO) satellite identifier.

  • earth_model ({"spherical", "elliptical"}, optional) – Surface model for the specular solver (default “spherical”).

  • max_central_angle_deg (float, keyword-only) – Maximum Tx-Rx geocentric central angle [deg]; a coarse geometric pre-filter. Required.

  • gnss_const (str, optional) – GNSS constellation label (GPS, GLONASS, GALILEO, BEIDOU).

time_vec¶

UTC timestamps of the samples.

Type:

numpy.ndarray

refl_ECI_vec¶

Specular points in ECI [m], shape (n, 3); NaN where no valid reflection.

Type:

numpy.ndarray

refl_ECEF_vec¶

Specular points in ECEF [m] (elliptical model only; None for spherical).

Type:

numpy.ndarray or None

refl_LL_vec¶

Specular points as (latitude, longitude) [deg], shape (n, 2).

Type:

numpy.ndarray

refl_ang_vec¶

Incidence angle at the reflection point wrt the local surface normal [deg], shape (n,).

Type:

numpy.ndarray

angle_diagnostics¶

Solver diagnostics [theta_in, theta_out, central_angle] per sample, shape (n, 3).

Type:

numpy.ndarray

link_budget¶

Link-budget output from compute_reflection_link_budget (empty in deferred mode).

Type:

dict

power¶

Received reflection power [W] per sample (None in deferred mode).

Type:

numpy.ndarray or None

compute_reflection_coordinates(GNSS_state, Sat_state, times, tx_eirp_dbw, antenna=None, frequency_hz=None, link_budget_settings=None, q_sat=None, compute_link_budget=True)[source]¶

Solve the specular point at every sample and (optionally) evaluate the link budget.

Fills the reflection attributes in place. The specular geometry is solved per earth_model (spherical closed form or elliptical stationary-path solve); samples failing the central-angle gate or the line-of-sight test are left as NaN.

Parameters:

  • GNSS_state (Satellite) – Propagated transmitting GNSS satellite (ECI positions / velocities).

  • Sat_state (Satellite) – Propagated receiving LEO satellite (ECI positions / velocities).

  • times (numpy.ndarray) – UTC timestamps aligned with the propagated states.

  • tx_eirp_dbw (float) – Transmit EIRP for this (constellation, band) [dBW].

  • antenna (RxAntenna or None, optional) – Receiver antenna (None => isotropic 0 dBi).

  • frequency_hz (float or None, optional) – Carrier frequency [Hz]; defaults to GPS L1.

  • link_budget_settings (dict or BistaticLinkBudgetSettings or None, optional) – Rx-system link-budget settings.

  • q_sat (numpy.ndarray or None, optional) – Attitude quaternion [w, x, y, z] (default identity).

  • compute_link_budget (bool, optional) – If False, skip the link budget (deferred per-event mode); default True.

get_reflection_point_ff(gnssPos, satPos, earth_radius=6371000.0)[source]¶

Specular point on a spherical Earth via the FreeFlyer method (the _ff suffix).

Rotates the Tx/Rx geometry into the orbital plane, solves the 2D specular point, and rotates back.

Parameters:

  • gnssPos (numpy.ndarray) – GNSS (Tx) satellite position [m], shape (3,).

  • satPos (numpy.ndarray) – Receiver (LEO) satellite position [m], shape (3,).

  • earth_radius (float, optional) – Sphere radius [m] (default Constants.R_EARTH_MEAN).

Returns:

(reflection_point, theta_degrees2, theta_degrees3): the 3D specular point (NaNs if no line of sight), the incidence angle and the reflected angle from the local normal [deg].

Return type:

tuple

get_rotation_3D_to_plane_coords(satCoord, GPSCoord)[source]¶

Rotation matrix mapping the Tx-Rx orbital plane onto the z = 0 plane.

static get_reflection_point2d(satCoord1, GPSCoord1, earth_radius=6371000.0)[source]¶

Specular point in the 2D orbital-plane frame (after rotation).

Solves the quartic that places the reflection on the circle while obeying the law of reflection.

Parameters:

  • satCoord1 (numpy.ndarray) – Receiver coordinates in the 2D plane (x, y) [m].

  • GPSCoord1 (numpy.ndarray) – GNSS coordinates in the 2D plane (x, y) [m].

  • earth_radius (float, optional) – Sphere radius [m] (default Constants.R_EARTH_MEAN).

Returns:

(N, A, B): the 2D reflection point [m] (None if no real positive root), and the normalised receiver and GNSS vectors.

Return type:

tuple

  • Gleason, S. & Gebre-Egziabher, D. (eds.), GNSS Applications and Methods, Artech House, 2009 (GNSS-R specular-point geometry).
